overview: This record is best understood as the Asian realm of Antigonus I, a powerful successor of Alexander the Great. Its broad eastern Mediterranean outline fits that setting better than the later Antigonid kingdom in Macedonia. However, the imported 300 to 200 BCE interval begins just after Antigonus died at Ipsus in 301 BCE. His power developed during the struggles after Alexander’s death in 323 BCE; the map cannot represent his kingdom surviving for another century.

periods.title: A successor’s expanding power
periods.summary: Alexander’s former general competed with other commanders for territory and influence.

periods.title: Antigonus and Demetrius as kings
periods.summary: Father and son adopted royal titles before the defeat at Ipsus.

periods.title: Demetrius continues separately
periods.summary: Antigonus’s son retained forces, later ruled Macedonia and died in captivity.

items.text: Antigonus had served Alexander before becoming a formidable rival to other successor generals. Appointed governor of Phrygia in 333 BCE, he already possessed an important base when Alexander died. His later kingdom grew from military command and competition among the successors.

Skepsis honored Antigonus after the peace of 311 BCE, planning sacrifices, a festival and citizens’ garlands. His sons received honors too: a public celebration could also advertise a political relationship.

After Demetrius’s naval victory in 306 BCE, Antigonus and his son adopted royal titles. Plutarch describes Antigonus sending Demetrius a diadem and a letter addressing him as king. Victory and family partnership helped turn commanders into a royal house.

Building naval power required many kinds of work. Diodorus describes Antigonus assembling woodcutters, sawyers and shipwrights in the mid-310s BCE, then bringing timber from Lebanon to the coast. Long before a sailor could pull an oar, someone had to fell, move and shape a tree.

The same account names shipyards at Tripolis, Byblos and Sidon, with another in Cilicia using timber from the Taurus mountains. Rhodes also agreed to build ships with imported wood. The fleet depended on a network of ports and supplies rather than one enormous royal workshop.

sections.title: What happened when a king planned to move a city?

items.text: Around 303 BCE, Antigonus proposed merging Lebedos with Teos. His letter required replacement building plots and temporary housing without rent while new homes were built. These were plans and instructions; the inscription does not prove that every household actually moved.

The envoys also worried about feeding a larger population. They requested a fund that traders could borrow against security to import grain. Antigonus initially preferred supplies from nearby royal land, but his letter ultimately allowed the proposed grain fund.

Combining cities meant combining rules. Teos and Lebedos agreed to borrow the laws of Kos temporarily, and Antigonus directed envoys to copy them and bring back a sealed version. Running the new community required paperwork as well as construction.

The letter even required a burial place for the people of Lebedos. A relocation plan had to make room for remembering relatives, not simply for streets and houses. This is a small but telling detail of civic and family life.

sections.title: Homes and water in an Ionian city

items.text: Priene offers a nearby archaeological comparison. Its town was laid out in the mid-fourth century BCE, before Antigonus’s royal title. A common house design arranged rooms around a courtyard, including a main living room and a room for entertaining. Family activities shared space with social visits.

Modern research at Priene challenges the idea that identical plots produced identical households. Even the earliest houses did not always follow the same plan, and property boundaries changed later. A tidy street grid was no guarantee that every family had the same space or resources.

Priene drew water from springs above the town through clay pipes, while channels along its streets carried wastewater away. These features belong to the city’s broader late-Classical and Hellenistic infrastructure. The hillside provided a useful water source, but keeping a town supplied still required pipes and maintenance.

Excavators at Priene carefully record objects room by room to understand how homes were used. Much surviving household material comes from a destruction around 140 to 130 BCE, long after Antigonus. Those later finds help reconstruct the city’s continuing life, but cannot simply be assigned to his reign.

sections.title: A written promise, a remembered victory and an ending

items.text: The Greek words “τοῖς Λεβεδίοις ἀμισθί”, transliterated tois Lebediois amisthi, mean “to the Lebedians without charge”. They come from the housing clause in Antigonus’s letter, around 303 BCE. This modern scholarly transcription preserves a practical promise of free accommodation.

A silver coin of Demetrius, dated 300 to 294 BCE, shows Nike, the goddess of victory, on a ship’s prow and Poseidon with his trident. Minted at Salamis on Cyprus, it recalls the naval victory of 306. The coin is later than Antigonus’s death: his son continued advertising the family’s achievements.

At Ipsus in 301 BCE, Antigonus faced an alliance of rival rulers. Plutarch describes Demetrius’s cavalry pursuing opponents too far and enemy elephants blocking its return. Antigonus was killed, and his Asian dominion broke apart. The account explains a military defeat, not the disappearance of its inhabitants.

ending.text: Antigonus died at Ipsus in 301 BCE and the victors divided his Asian realm. Demetrius survived and later ruled Macedonia; the family continued there in later generations. The imported 200 BCE endpoint is not Antigonus I’s fall, and his kingdom must be distinguished from later Antigonid Macedonia.
